<!-- theoremx-1: body_md -->
\label{t:A}
The inclusion $C^*_r(P_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$ is $\mathcal{Z}$-stable and selfless. Hence every intermediate inclusion and every intermediate $C^*$-algebra is $\mathcal{Z}$-stable and selfless. In particular each intermediate $C^*$-algebra is simple with a unique tracial state, and it has stable rank one and strict comparison.
<!-- end theoremx-1 -->
<!-- theoremx-2: body_md -->
\label{t:B}
The inclusion $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$ is selfless. Hence every intermediate inclusion and every intermediate $C^*$-algebra is selfless.
<!-- end theoremx-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{t:criterion}
Let $H\leq G$ be countable groups. Suppose that $H\cap C_G(E)$ contains a copy of $\mathbb{F}_2$ for every finite set $E\subseteq G$. Then there is a unital embedding $\mathcal{Z}\toC^*_r(H)_\infty\capC^*_r(G)'$. Consequently $C^*_r(H)\subseteqC^*_r(G)$ and all its intermediate inclusions and $C^*$-algebras are $\mathcal{Z}$-stable.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Choose finite sets $E_1\subseteq E_2\subseteq\dotsb$ with union $G$. Choose $F_k\leq H\cap C_G(E_k)$ with $F_k\simeq\mathbb{F}_2$. There are unital embeddings $\varphi_k\colon\mathcal{Z}\toC^*_r(F_k)\subseteqC^*_r(H)$ \cite[Proposition~4.2 and Remark~4.3]{ThW14}. Each $\lambda(g)$ commutes with the image of $\varphi_k$ for large $k$. These elements span a dense subspace of $C^*_r(G)$. Hence $\lVert[\varphi_k(c),a]\rVert\to0$ for all $c\in\mathcal{Z}$ and $a\inC^*_r(G)$. Thus the $\varphi_k$ induce a unital $*$-homomorphism $\mathcal{Z}\toC^*_r(H)_\infty\capC^*_r(G)'$. It is injective since $\mathcal{Z}$ is simple.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{p:inner}
Let $C$ be a central subgroup of a countable group $G$ such that $G/C$ is not inner amenable. Let $\sigma$ be a $2$-cocycle on $G$ such that $C^*_r(C,\sigma)$ is commutative. Then $C^*_r(G,\sigma)$ is not $\mathcal{Z}$-stable. In particular $C^*_r(G,\sigma)$ is not $\mathcal{Z}$-stable for any $\sigma$ when $G$ is not inner amenable.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Put $A=C^*_r(G,\sigma)$ and $Q=G/C$, and suppose that $A$ is $\mathcal{Z}$-stable. Since $\mathcal{Z}\simeq\mathcal{Z}^{\otimes\infty}$, there is a unital $*$-homomorphism $\varphi\colon\mathcal{Z}\to A_\infty\cap A'$. Let $\omega$ be a free ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$. Then $(x_j)_j\mapsto\lim_\omega\tau(x_j)$ is a tracial state on $A_\infty$. Its composition with $\varphi$ is the unique tracial state of $\mathcal{Z}$, which is faithful. Choose $a,b\in\mathcal{Z}$ with $ab\neq ba$. Lift $\varphi(a)$ and $\varphi(b)$ to bounded sequences $(a_j)$ and $(b_j)$ in $A$. Then $\lVert[a_j,x]\rVert\to0$ and $\lVert[b_j,x]\rVert\to0$ for all $x\in A$, but $\lim_\omega\lVert[a_j,b_j]\rVert_2>0$.

Let $E\colon A\toC^*_r(C,\sigma)$ be the conditional expectation that keeps the Fourier coefficients on $C$. For $x\in A$ and $q\in Q$ put $\xi_x(q)=(\sum_{g\in q}\lvert\hat x(g)\rvert^2)^{1/2}$. Then $\lVert x-E(x)\rVert_2$ is the norm of the restriction of $\xi_x$ to $Q\setminus\{e\}$. The coefficient of $\lambda_\sigma(h)x\lambda_\sigma(h)^*$ at $hgh^{-1}$ has modulus $\lvert\hat x(g)\rvert$. Hence
\[
\lVert\lambda_\sigma(h)x\lambda_\sigma(h)^*-x\rVert_2\geq\lVert h\cdot\xi_x-\xi_x\rVert_2,
\]
where $(h\cdot\xi)(q)=\xi(h^{-1}qh)$. Since $Q$ is not inner amenable, there are $h_1,\dotsc,h_m\in G$ and $\kappa>0$ with $\sum_i\lVert h_i\cdot\eta-\eta\rVert_2\geq\kappa\lVert\eta\rVert_2$ for all $\eta\in\ell^2(Q\setminus\{e\})$, see \cite{Ef75}. Hence $\kappa\lVert x-E(x)\rVert_2\leq\sum_i\lVert\lambda_\sigma(h_i)x\lambda_\sigma(h_i)^*-x\rVert_2$ for all $x\in A$. So $\lVert a_j-E(a_j)\rVert_2\to0$ and $\lVert b_j-E(b_j)\rVert_2\to0$. Since $C^*_r(C,\sigma)$ is commutative and $E$ is contractive, $\lVert[a_j,b_j]\rVert_2\to0$. This is a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{l:center}
Let $n\geq3$. Then $Z(B_n)\cap B_{n-1}=\{e\}$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Suppose $z_n^l\in B_{n-1}$. Then $z_n^l\in P_n\cap B_{n-1}=P_{n-1}$. So its class has coefficient zero at $a_{1,n}$. But this coefficient is $l$, so $l=0$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{l:tails}
Let $k\geq1$. Then $T_k=\langle s_{k+1}^2,s_{k+2}^2\rangle\leq P_\infty$ is free of rank two, and it commutes with $B_k$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The generators $s_{k+1}$ and $s_{k+2}$ commute with $s_1,\dotsc,s_{k-1}$. Conjugation by $(s_1\dotsm s_{k+2})^k$ maps $s_1$ and $s_2$ to $s_{k+1}$ and $s_{k+2}$ \cite{KT08}. In $B_3/Z(B_3)\simeq\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ the elements $s_1^2$ and $s_2^2$ map to the classes of
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-2&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
These generate a free group of rank two. Hence $T_k$ is free on $s_{k+1}^2$ and $s_{k+2}^2$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{c:braids}
Let $P_\infty'=[P_\infty,P_\infty]$. Then $C^*_r(P_\infty')\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$ is $\mathcal{Z}$-stable. Hence every intermediate inclusion and every intermediate $C^*$-algebra is $\mathcal{Z}$-stable.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
A finite subset of $B_\infty$ lies in some $B_k$. By Lemma~\ref{l:tails} the group $T_k\leq P_\infty$ commutes with $B_k$. The group $[T_k,T_k]\leq P_\infty'$ is free of infinite rank. So it contains a copy of $\mathbb{F}_2$. Now apply Theorem~\ref{t:criterion}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{p:free}
Let $n\geq3$ and let $\beta\in B_{n+1}$ be pseudo-Anosov. Then $\langle B_n,\beta^N\rangle=B_n*\langle\beta^N\rangle$ for all large $N$. Such $\beta$ exist in $\mathbb{F}_n=\langle a_{1,2},\dotsc,a_{1,n+1}\rangle$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Put $q=q_{n+1}$, $H=q(B_n)$, and $f=q(\beta)$. The map $q$ is injective on $B_n$ by Lemma~\ref{l:center}. Hence $H$ is infinite and torsion-free. The sphere $S$ has $n+2\geq5$ punctures. So $\operatorname{Mod}(S)$ acts acylindrically on its curve graph, and $f$ is loxodromic. The group $H$ fixes the curve around $p_1,\dotsc,p_n$. This curve is essential since both sides contain at least two punctures. Thus $H$ is elliptic.

We check the two conditions of \cite[Proposition~2.1]{AD19}. Let $\delta$ be a hyperbolicity constant. Let $\operatorname{Fix}_{50\delta}(H)$ be the set of points that every $h\in H$ moves at most $50\delta$. Suppose it contains two points at distance at least $R$. Then infinitely many elements of $H$ move both points at most $50\delta$. For large $R$ this contradicts acylindricity. Hence $\operatorname{Fix}_{50\delta}(H)$ is bounded, and it meets a quasi-axis of $f$ in a bounded set. Next let $E(f)$ be the stabilizer of the two fixed points of $f$ on the boundary. It is virtually cyclic \cite{DGO}. Thus $\langle f\rangle$ has finite index in $E(f)$, and the elements of infinite order in $E(f)$ are loxodromic. The elements of $H$ are elliptic and $H$ is torsion-free. Hence $H\cap E(f)=\{e\}$. Consequently no $h\neq e$ in $H$ preserves a quasi-axis of $f$, since such $h$ would lie in $E(f)$. Now \cite[Proposition~2.1]{AD19} gives $\langle H,f^N\rangle=H*\langle f^N\rangle$ for all large $N$. The natural map $B_n*\langle\beta^N\rangle\to B_{n+1}$ composed with $q$ is an isomorphism onto $H*\langle f^N\rangle$. So the natural map is injective.

Forgetting the first string maps the braids in $B_{n+1}$ that fix the first string onto the braid group of the other $n$ strings. Its kernel is $\mathbb{F}_n$ \cite[Corollary~1.23]{KT08}. Let $S'$ be the sphere obtained from $S$ by filling in $p_1$. Moving $p_1$ once along a loop in $S'$ gives a mapping class of $S$, called a point push \cite[Chapter~4]{FM}. Under $q$ the group $\mathbb{F}_n$ becomes the group of point pushes of $p_1$. A loop in $S'$ is \emph{filling} if it cannot be homotoped off any essential simple closed curve in $S'$. Since $S'$ has $n+1\geq4$ punctures, such loops exist. The point push of $p_1$ along a filling loop is pseudo-Anosov \cite[Chapter~14]{FM}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{l:free}
Let $H\leq G$ be countable groups. Suppose that for every finite set $E\subseteq G$ there is $g\in H$ of infinite order with $\langle E,g\rangle=\langle E\rangle*\langle g\rangle$. Then $C^*_r(H)\subseteqC^*_r(G)$ is a selfless inclusion.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Choose finite sets $E_k$ that increase to $G$ and elements $g_k\in H$ as above. Put $G_k=\langle E_k\rangle$. An alternating product of nontrivial elements of $G_k$ and $\langle g_k\rangle$ is nontrivial. So $C^*_r(G_k)$ and $C^*_r(\langle g_k\rangle)$ are free with respect to $\tau$. Let $C(\mathbb{T})$ carry the Haar state, that is, integration against normalized Lebesgue measure. Let $u\in C(\mathbb{T})$ be the identity function. Since $g_k$ has infinite order, there is a trace-preserving isomorphism $C(\mathbb{T})\toC^*_r(\langle g_k\rangle)$ that sends $u$ to $\lambda(g_k)$. This gives trace-preserving embeddings
\[
\Psi_k\colonC^*_r(G_k)*C(\mathbb{T})\toC^*_r(G)
\]
that fix $C^*_r(G_k)$ and send $u$ to $\lambda(g_k)$. The algebras $C^*_r(G_k)*C(\mathbb{T})$ increase and their union is dense in $C^*_r(G)*C(\mathbb{T})$. Each $x$ in the union lies in the domain of $\Psi_k$ for all large $k$. Let $\Psi(x)$ be the class of $(\Psi_k(x))_k$ in $C^*_r(G)^\omega$, with arbitrary entries for small $k$. Then $\Psi$ is a trace-preserving $*$-homomorphism. It is isometric since $\lVert\Psi_k(x)\rVert=\lVert x\rVert$ for large $k$. Hence $\Psi$ extends to $C^*_r(G)*C(\mathbb{T})$. It is the diagonal embedding on $C^*_r(G)$, and $\Psi(u)\inC^*_r(H)^\omega$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $E\subseteq B_\infty$ be finite. Choose $n\geq3$ with $E\subseteq B_n$. Proposition~\ref{p:free} gives $g\in\mathbb{F}_n$ with $\langle B_n,g\rangle=B_n*\langle g\rangle$. Then $\langle E,g\rangle=\langle E\rangle*\langle g\rangle$ and $g\in\mathbb{F}_\infty$. Therefore Lemma~\ref{l:free} applies.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Every intermediate inclusion of $C^*_r(P_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$ is also an intermediate inclusion of $C^*_r(P_\infty')\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$ and of $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$. So it is $\mathcal{Z}$-stable by Corollary~\ref{c:braids} and selfless by Theorem~\ref{t:B}. The last statement follows from \cite[Theorem~3.1]{Ro25}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{r:pams}
The selflessness in Theorem~\ref{t:A} also follows from the $\mathcal{Z}$-stability. Each $P_n$ is an iterated semidirect product of free groups \cite[Section~1]{Om20}. So $B_n$ and $B_\infty$ are exact \cite{BO08}. Each intermediate $C^*$-algebra is some $C^*_r(\Gamma)$, and it is simple \cite[Example~7.4]{BO23}. So it has a unique tracial state \cite{BKKO}. It is also exact and $\mathcal{Z}$-stable. Hence it is selfless by \cite[Theorem~3]{Oz}. For the inclusion, note that the triple $(B_\infty,P_\infty,1)$ satisfies the relative Kleppner condition \cite[Section~6]{Om20}. Moreover $P_\infty$ is $C^*$-simple, so $C^*_r(P_\infty)$ has a unique tracial state \cite{BKKO}. Hence $C^*_r(P_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$ has the relative Dixmier property \cite[Theorem~6.2]{BO23}. That is, $\tau(a)1$ lies in the closed convex hull of $\{uau^*:u\in U(C^*_r(P_\infty))\}$ for every $a\inC^*_r(B_\infty)$. Now \cite[Theorem~2.9]{HKEPR} shows that the $\mathcal{Z}$-stable inclusion $C^*_r(P_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$ is selfless. A similar route gives selfless inclusions for amenable groups in \cite{Om26}. Here the $\mathcal{Z}$-stability comes from Theorem~\ref{t:criterion} instead.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{r:irred}
The subgroup $\mathbb{F}_\infty$ is normal in $P_\infty$, but not in $B_\infty$. For instance $s_1a_{1,3}s_1^{-1}=a_{2,3}\notin\mathbb{F}_\infty$. Nevertheless $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$ is $C^*$-irreducible. Indeed every intermediate $C^*$-algebra is selfless by Theorem~\ref{t:B}, hence simple \cite[Theorem~3.1]{Ro25}. Moreover the inclusion has the relative Dixmier property \cite[Theorem~2.5(iv)]{HKEPR}. This complements \cite[Example~7.4]{BO23}, where the subgroup $P_\infty$ is normal.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{r:php}
Selflessness of $C^*_r(B_\infty)$ alone also follows from Ozawa's property $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{PHP}}$ \cite[Section~8]{Oz}. Let $F\subseteq B_\infty$ be finite and choose $n\geq3$ with $F\subseteq B_n$. The group $Q=q_{n+1}(B_{n+1})$ has finite index in the mapping class group of a sphere with $n+2\geq5$ punctures. So it is acylindrically hyperbolic. Its finite radical is trivial, since $Q\simeq B_{n+1}/Z(B_{n+1})$ is $C^*$-simple \cite[Remark~2.1]{Om20}. Hence $Q$ satisfies the hypothesis of \cite[Proposition~15]{Oz} by \cite[Proposition~0.3]{AD19}, as noted in \cite[Section~8]{Oz}. Let $B_{n+1}$ act through $q_{n+1}$. By Lemma~\ref{l:center} every element of $B_n\setminus\{e\}$ acts nontrivially. So the proof of \cite[Proposition~15]{Oz} gives the elements $t_i$ and the sets $C_i\subseteq D_i$ required in $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{PHP}}$ for $F$, with $B_{n+1}$ in place of $B_\infty$. Let $R$ be a set of representatives for the right cosets of $B_{n+1}$ in $B_\infty$. Then the same $t_i$ and the sets $C_iR\subseteq D_iR$ satisfy $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{PHP}}$ for $F$ in $B_\infty$. Hence $B_\infty$ has property $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{PHP}}$, and $C^*_r(B_\infty)$ is completely selfless \cite[Theorem~14]{Oz}. This does not directly give the inclusions in Theorems~\ref{t:A} and~\ref{t:B}. For them the elements $t_i$ would have to lie in $P_\infty$ or in $\mathbb{F}_\infty$, compare \cite[Section~3]{HKEPR}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{l:scalars}
Let $h\in G$. For $t\in C_G(h)$ put $\chi_h(t)=\sigma(t,h)\overline{\sigma(h,t)}$. Then $\chi_h$ is a character on $C_G(h)$. Hence $\lambda_\sigma(t)$ commutes with $\lambda_\sigma(h)$ for all $t\in[C_G(h),C_G(h)]$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
For $t\in C_G(h)$ we have $\lambda_\sigma(t)\lambda_\sigma(h)=\chi_h(t)\lambda_\sigma(h)\lambda_\sigma(t)$. Applying this to $t_1$, $t_2$, and $t_1t_2$ gives $\chi_h(t_1t_2)=\chi_h(t_1)\chi_h(t_2)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{t:twisted}
Let $H\leq G$ be countable groups and let $\sigma$ be a $2$-cocycle on $G$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Under the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{t:criterion} there is a unital embedding
\[
\mathcal{Z}\toC^*_r(H,\sigma)_\infty\capC^*_r(G,\sigma)'.
\]
So $C^*_r(H,\sigma)\subseteqC^*_r(G,\sigma)$ and all its intermediate inclusions and $C^*$-algebras are $\mathcal{Z}$-stable.
\item[(b)] Under the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{l:free} the inclusion $C^*_r(H,\sigma)\subseteqC^*_r(G,\sigma)$ is selfless.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
(a) Let $E_k$ and $F_k$ be as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{t:criterion}. Choose $K_k\leq[F_k,F_k]$ with $K_k\simeq\mathbb{F}_2$. By Lemma~\ref{l:scalars} the unitaries $\lambda_\sigma(t)$ with $t\in K_k$ commute with $\lambda_\sigma(g)$ for all $g\in E_k$. Every $2$-cocycle on a free group is a coboundary. So $C^*_r(K_k,\sigma)\simeqC^*_r(\mathbb{F}_2)$, and the proof of Theorem~\ref{t:criterion} applies to the groups $K_k$.

(b) Let $G_k$ and $g_k$ be as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:free}. Let $x_1,\dotsc,x_r$ be nontrivial elements taken alternately from $G_k$ and $\langle g_k\rangle$. Then $\lambda_\sigma(x_1)\dotsm\lambda_\sigma(x_r)$ is a scalar multiple of $\lambda_\sigma(x_1\dotsm x_r)$, and $x_1\dotsm x_r\neq e$. So its trace is zero. Hence $C^*_r(G_k,\sigma)$ and $C^*_r(\langle g_k\rangle,\sigma)$ are free with respect to $\tau$. Moreover $\lambda_\sigma(g_k)^n$ is a scalar multiple of $\lambda_\sigma(g_k^n)$, so its trace is zero for $n\neq0$. So $u\mapsto\lambda_\sigma(g_k)$ defines a trace-preserving isomorphism $C(\mathbb{T})\toC^*_r(\langle g_k\rangle,\sigma)$. Now the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:free} applies.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{c:twisted}
Let $\Gamma\leq B_\infty$ and let $\sigma$ be a $2$-cocycle on $\Gamma$, which need not extend to $B_\infty$ (Example~\ref{ex:scalars}). If $P_\infty'\leq\Gamma$, then $C^*_r(P_\infty',\sigma)\subseteqC^*_r(\Gamma,\sigma)$ is $\mathcal{Z}$-stable. If $\mathbb{F}_\infty\leq\Gamma$, then $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty,\sigma)\subseteqC^*_r(\Gamma,\sigma)$ is selfless. In both cases every intermediate inclusion and every intermediate $C^*$-algebra has the same property. In particular $C^*_r(P_\infty,\sigma)\subseteqC^*_r(\Gamma,\sigma)$ is $\mathcal{Z}$-stable and selfless when $P_\infty\leq\Gamma$. Its intermediate $C^*$-algebras are then exactly the algebras $C^*_r(\Gamma',\sigma)$ with $P_\infty\leq\Gamma'\leq\Gamma$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The proofs of Corollary~\ref{c:braids} and Theorem~\ref{t:B} apply with $B_\infty$ replaced by $\Gamma$, and with Theorem~\ref{t:twisted} in place of Theorem~\ref{t:criterion} and Lemma~\ref{l:free}. Intermediate inclusions are handled as in Sections~\ref{sec:criterion} and~\ref{sec:selfless}. For the last part note that $P_\infty$ is normal in $\Gamma$ and $C^*$-simple. Moreover every nontrivial element of $B_\infty$ has an infinite $P_\infty$-conjugacy class \cite[Section~6]{Om20}. Hence $C^*_r(P_\infty,\sigma)$ is simple \cite[Corollary~4.5]{BK}, and $(\Gamma,P_\infty,\sigma)$ satisfies the relative Kleppner condition. Now \cite[Theorem~6.2]{BO23} gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:scalars}
Commutators cannot be avoided in general. The abelianization of $P_\infty$ is free abelian on the classes of the $a_{i,j}$. Let $\ell_{i,j}\colon P_\infty\to\mathbb{Z}$ be the corresponding coordinate maps. Put $\mu=\ell_{1,2}$ and $\nu=\sum_{i\geq3}\ell_{i,i+1}$. The sum is finite on each braid. For $\theta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$ the bicharacter $\sigma(g,h)=e^{2\pi i\theta\mu(g)\nu(h)}$ is a $2$-cocycle on $P_\infty$. For $i\geq3$ the braids $a_{1,2}$ and $a_{i,i+1}$ commute. But
\[
\lambda_\sigma(a_{1,2})\lambda_\sigma(a_{i,i+1})=e^{2\pi i\theta}\lambda_\sigma(a_{i,i+1})\lambda_\sigma(a_{1,2}).
\]
So $\lambda_\sigma(a_{1,2})$ does not commute with $\lambda_\sigma(a_{i,i+1})$, however large $i$ is. In particular $\sigma$ is not a coboundary. If $2\theta\notin\mathbb{Z}$, then $\sigma$ is not cohomologous to the restriction of a $2$-cocycle on $B_\infty$. Indeed conjugation by $\Delta_{i+1}$ interchanges $a_{1,2}=s_1^2$ and $a_{i,i+1}=s_i^2$ \cite{KT08}. For a $2$-cocycle on $B_\infty$ the scalar $e^{2\pi i\theta}$ above would then equal its inverse.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{l:annular}
The assignment $a_{1,j}\mapsto x_{j-1}$ and $s_k\mapsto s_{k-1}$ for $j,k\geq2$ defines an isomorphism $A_\infty\simeq\mathbb{F}_\infty\rtimes_\alpha B_\infty$. Its restriction to $P_\infty$ is the isomorphism $P_\infty\simeq\mathbb{F}_\infty\rtimes_\alpha P_\infty$ of \cite[Section~6]{Om20}.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Forgetting the first string maps $A_\infty$ onto the braid group of the strings $2,3,\dotsc$ with kernel $\langle a_{1,j}:j\geq2\rangle$ \cite[Corollary~1.23]{KT08}. The subgroup $\langle s_2,s_3,\dotsc\rangle\simeq B_\infty$ is a section. For $k\geq2$ we have
\[
s_ka_{1,k}s_k^{-1}=a_{1,k+1},\qquad s_ka_{1,k+1}s_k^{-1}=a_{1,k+1}^{-1}a_{1,k}a_{1,k+1},
\]
and $s_ka_{1,j}s_k^{-1}=a_{1,j}$ for $j\notin\{k,k+1\}$. The first identity is the definition of $a_{1,k+1}$. Since $s_k^2=a_{k,k+1}$, the second is equivalent to the relation $a_{1,k}a_{1,k+1}a_{k,k+1}=a_{1,k+1}a_{k,k+1}a_{1,k}$ \cite[Lemma~1.8.2]{Bi74}. For $j<k$ the third is clear. For $j\geq k+2$ write $a_{1,j}=ws_1^2w^{-1}$ with $w=s_{j-1}\dotsm s_2$. Then $s_kw=ws_{k+1}$, and $s_{k+1}$ commutes with $s_1$. These identities are \cite[(1.1)]{Om20} for $\alpha(s_{k-1})$ after the substitution $x_{j-1}=a_{1,j}$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{c:artin}
Let $\Lambda\leq B_\infty$ and $\varphi\in Z^1(\Lambda,\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{F}_\infty,\mathbb{T}))$. Then $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\rtimes^r_{\alpha^\varphi}\Lambda$ is a selfless inclusion. If $P_\infty\leq\Lambda$, then $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\rtimes^r_{\alpha^\varphi}\Lambda$ is also $\mathcal{Z}$-stable.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We have $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\rtimes^r_{\alpha^\varphi}\Lambda\simeqC^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty\rtimes_\alpha\Lambda,\sigma^\varphi)$, and this identifies $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)$ with $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty,\sigma^\varphi)=C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)$ \cite[Section~2.2]{Om20}. By Lemma~\ref{l:annular} the group $\mathbb{F}_\infty\rtimes_\alpha\Lambda$ is isomorphic to a subgroup $\Gamma$ of $B_\infty$ with $\mathbb{F}_\infty\leq\Gamma$. If $P_\infty\leq\Lambda$, then also $P_\infty\leq\Gamma$. Now apply Corollary~\ref{c:twisted}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{r:galois}
The inclusion in Corollary~\ref{c:artin} is $C^*$-irreducible, since its intermediate $C^*$-algebras are selfless and hence simple \cite[Theorem~3.1]{Ro25}. So by the Galois correspondence of \cite[Theorem~4.4]{CS19}, see \cite[Theorem~5.2]{BO23}, every intermediate $C^*$-algebra equals $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\rtimes^r_{\alpha^\varphi}\Lambda'$ for a unique subgroup $\Lambda'\leq\Lambda$. For $\Lambda=B_\infty$ and trivial $\varphi$, Lemma~\ref{l:annular} shows that the intermediate $C^*$-algebras of $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(A_\infty)$ are exactly the algebras $C^*_r(\Gamma)$ with $\mathbb{F}_\infty\leq\Gamma\leq A_\infty$. We do not know whether the same holds for $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_\infty)\subseteqC^*_r(B_\infty)$, where $\mathbb{F}_\infty$ is not normal (Remark~\ref{r:irred}). For nonnormal subgroups the correspondence can fail, even for $C^*$-irreducible inclusions. For instance $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_2)\subseteqC^*_r(\mathbb{F}_3)$ is $C^*$-irreducible \cite[Example~5.4]{Ror23}, where $\mathbb{F}_3=\langle x_1,x_2,x_3\rangle$ and $\mathbb{F}_2=\langle x_1,x_2\rangle$. Let $E$ be generated by $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_2)$ and $\lambda(x_3)+\lambda(x_3)^*$. By freeness, the conditional expectation onto $C^*_r(\langle x_3\rangle)$ maps $E$ into $C^*(\lambda(x_3)+\lambda(x_3)^*)$, which does not contain $\lambda(x_3)$. So $\lambda(x_3)\notin E$, and hence $E\neqC^*_r(\Gamma)$ for every $\Gamma$. For von Neumann algebras compare \cite[Remark~4.5]{BO23}.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{p:finite}
Let $2\leq n<\infty$ and let $\varphi\in Z^1(K,\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{F}_n,\mathbb{T}))$, where $K=B_n$ or $K=P_n$. Then $C^*_r(\mathbb{F}_n)\rtimes^r_{\alpha^\varphi}K$ is not $\mathcal{Z}$-stable.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Put $G=\mathbb{F}_n\rtimes_\alpha K$ and $\sigma=\sigma^\varphi$. The center $C$ of $G$ is infinite cyclic \cite[Section~1]{Om20}, so $C^*_r(C,\sigma)$ is commutative. The quotient $G/C$ is a $C^*$-simple subgroup of finite index in $B_{n+1}/Z(B_{n+1})$ \cite[Remark~2.1]{Om20}. As above, it is not inner amenable. So $C^*_r(G,\sigma)$ is not $\mathcal{Z}$-stable by Proposition~\ref{p:inner}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{p:stable}
The reduced group $C^*$-algebras of the following groups are $\mathcal{Z}$-stable.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] The Artin group of a Coxeter graph with countably many vertices, each of finite degree, and infinitely many edges.
\item[(b)] The groups $\mathrm{SL}_\infty(\mathbb{Z})$, $\mathrm{GL}_\infty(\mathbb{Z})$, and $\mathrm{Sp}_\infty(\mathbb{Z})$, that is, the increasing unions of $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$, $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$, and $\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}(\mathbb{Z})$ under the standard embeddings.
\item[(c)] The group $\operatorname{Aut}_f\mathbb{F}_\infty$ of automorphisms of $\mathbb{F}_\infty=\langle x_1,x_2,\dotsc\rangle$ that fix all but finitely many $x_i$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
In each case every finite subset of the group lies in a subgroup that commutes with a copy of $\mathbb{F}_2$. Then Theorem~\ref{t:criterion} applies.

(a) Let $V_0$ be a finite set of vertices. Only finitely many edges meet $V_0$ or its neighbors. So we can choose an edge $\{u,v\}$ that meets neither. Then $s_u$ and $s_v$ commute with $s_w$ for all $w\in V_0$. Moreover $s_u^2$ and $s_v^2$ generate a free group of rank two \cite{CP01}. For $B_\infty$ this is Lemma~\ref{l:tails}.

(b) The group $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ commutes with the block-diagonal copy of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ in the next two coordinates, and $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ contains $\mathbb{F}_2$. The same works for $\mathrm{GL}$ and for $\mathrm{Sp}$, since $\mathrm{Sp}_2(\mathbb{Z})=\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$.

(c) Automorphisms of $\langle x_1,\dotsc,x_n\rangle$ commute with automorphisms of $\langle x_{n+1},x_{n+2}\rangle$, all extended by the identity. The inner automorphisms of $\langle x_{n+1},x_{n+2}\rangle$ form a free group of rank two.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{r:stable}
If a group $G$ as above is also $C^*$-simple and exact, then $C^*_r(G)$ has a unique tracial state \cite{BKKO}. So it is selfless by \cite[Theorem~3]{Oz}. For instance $\mathrm{SL}_\infty(\mathbb{Z})$ is the increasing union of the $C^*$-simple groups $\mathrm{SL}_{2k+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ \cite{BCdlH}. So it is $C^*$-simple. Then $\mathrm{GL}_\infty(\mathbb{Z})$ is $C^*$-simple by \cite[Theorem~1.4]{BKKO}, since the centralizer of $\mathrm{SL}_\infty(\mathbb{Z})$ in it is trivial. Both groups are exact as increasing unions of linear groups \cite{BO08}. Hence $C^*_r(\mathrm{SL}_\infty(\mathbb{Z}))$ and $C^*_r(\mathrm{GL}_\infty(\mathbb{Z}))$ are simple, $\mathcal{Z}$-stable, and selfless. They are also singly generated \cite[Theorem~3.7]{ThW14}. For $\mathrm{SL}_\infty(\mathbb{Z})$ the selflessness also follows from \cite{Vi} and \cite[Theorem~4.1]{Ro25}.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
